Heat wave to spread across Romania from July 30, peak expected in early August
A heat wave is expected to spread across Romania from July 30, bringing increasingly hot weather and heat stress across much of the country, with the most intense conditions forecast between August 3 and 6, according to the National Meteorological Administration (ANM). The weather agency also issued a yellow heat warning for seven western and southwestern counties valid from Thursday morning through Friday morning.
The yellow warning is in effect from 10:00 a.m. on July 30 until 10:00 a.m. on July 31 for the counties of Dolj, Mehedinți, Caraș-Severin, Timiș, Arad, Bihor, and Satu Mare. Maximum temperatures will range from 33 to 37 degrees Celsius, with the highest values forecast in the Western Plain.
For the coming days, the meteorologists said the hottest weather will initially affect the country's western regions before gradually expanding eastward.
“From July 30, we will be talking about a heat wave that will gradually expand and intensify across our country, starting from the western regions, with its maximum intensity most likely between August 3 and 6," ANM said.
Temperatures in the regions of Banat and Crișana are expected to reach 35-36 degrees Celsius on Thursday, July 30, rising to 37-38 degrees on Friday, with isolated highs of up to 39 degrees Celsius.
Then, during the weekend of August 1-2, temperatures around 35 degrees Celsius are also expected locally in Maramureș, Transylvania, and Oltenia, and in isolated areas of Muntenia and Moldova. Heat discomfort is also forecast to increase gradually, first in western Romania and then across other parts of the country.
According to ANM, weather models indicate that maximum temperatures in western Romania could remain around 38-39 degrees Celsius until approximately August 6 before beginning to ease. In southern Romania, however, the hottest conditions are expected to develop later, from around August 3, and could persist until around August 9.
The meteorological agency noted that, despite its nickname as Romania's hottest month, July has so far been relatively moderate this year.
“Up to this point, July has not seen significant temperature extremes, with very few periods of heatwave conditions," ANM said, adding that the country's average temperature up to July 27 stood at 20.2 degrees Celsius, 0.1 degrees below the 1991-2020 average and lower than in each of the previous three years.
ANM attributed the upcoming heat wave to a persistent high-pressure system over much of Europe combined with the advance of very warm North African air across southern and southeastern parts of the continent, creating conditions for prolonged hot and dry weather.

SEOUL, July 29 (Yonhap) -- The state weather agency issued a heat wave warning for most parts of Seoul on Wednesday, marking the capital's second alert of its kind this summer.
The Korea Meteorological Administration (KMA) upgraded a heat wave advisory to a full warning for eastern and southwestern parts of Seoul at 11 a.m., as a nationwide heat wave has recently gripped the country.
The agency issued the capital's first heat wave warning this summer on July 11.
A heat wave warning is issued when the maximum apparent temperature is expected to remain above 35 C for two or more consecutive days.
The apparent temperature reached 34.8 C in southern Seoul at 1 p.m., according to the KMA.
The agency attributed the heat wave to the dual influence of the North Pacific High and the Tibetan High pressure systems, projecting the heat wave to persist through the end of next week.
In response, the Seoul metropolitan government has opened local administrative offices for the public to use to cool off around the clock.
The city has also restricted outdoor work from 2 to 5 p.m. at municipal construction sites, recommending private construction sites to do the same.

Experts at a Surrey gardens have given advice on how to treat plants as a fourth heatwave gets under way in the South East.
The Royal Horticultural Society's (RHS) Wisley garden in Surrey, which has had no rain for nearly six weeks, said while it was being affected by the dry weather, planting had evolved to stand up to drought.
RHS horticulture director, Tim Upson, said the plant trials part of the garden showed Persian roses and baptisia were drought tolerance winners while sweet peas were losers.
The UK Health and Security Agency heat-health alert for South East England rose to amber, prompting Ashford & St. Peter's Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust to ask visitors to bring cool water.
Many areas of the Wisley garden were being left without irrigation, to minimise water use to ensure crops, and the garden was beginning to see leaves fall off on cherries and other plants.
But Upson said wild carrots were "looking great", and crape myrtles were flowering well in the heat.
He added: "We have future-proofed with such plantings so we have colour even in the heat and drought by making the right selections."
RHS chief horticulturist, Guy Barter, said gardeners across Kent, Surrey and Sussex could follow Wisley's lead by focusing on watering plants which must be watered, and composting or cutting back anything "past the point of no return".
He said: "It is also worth delaying summer seed sowing to prioritise water where it's already needed and think about what you should grow in 2027 - perhaps prioritise those crops less readily available in the shops and less thirsty.
"It's all about eking out the last of the water supply you might have in your garden until daylight hours reduce next month and plants become less thirsty."

Amber and yellow heat health alerts are in force as parts of the UK endure the fourth widespread heatwave of the year so far.
Temperatures are forecast to peak on Wednesday with readings as high as 35C (95F) in the hottest places.
Though the heatwave will come to a quick end for many on Thursday, well above-average temperatures in the mid- to high 20s Celsius will persist into the weekend.
The hot weather, paired with a significant lack of rainfall, will exacerbate conditions in many of the driest areas.
How hot will it get where you live?
A plume of intense heat surging north from North Africa, and already bringing exceptionally high temperatures to parts of Iberia and France, will reach the UK on Wednesday.
Temperatures are expected to climb sharply across southern and eastern England and into parts of the Midlands, marking the peak of a short but notable heatwave.
Temperatures in these areas will range from 30-35C at their highest point on Wednesday.
Some eastern areas of Wales could also edge into heatwave criteria.
The UK Health Security Agency has issued amber heat health alerts for the East Midlands, East of England, London and the south-east from 09:00 BST on 29 July until 09:00 BST on 30 July.
The alert warns that significant impacts are likely across health and social care services due to the high temperatures, including a rise in deaths, particularly among those aged 65 and over or with health conditions.
Less severe yellow heat heat alerts have also been issued for the same period for the south-west, West Midlands, and Yorkshire and the Humber.
For much of Wales and Northern England, the three-day run of temperatures of 25C or above required to classify as a heatwave will not be met.
The same is true for Scotland and Northern Ireland where temperatures will rise closer to 20C at best.
How long will the heat last?
This time around the heat spike looks set to be brief.
The hottest conditions will be concentrated on Wednesday before a weather front moving through on Thursday will usher in fresher air, bringing a noticeable change in feel.
Temperatures are expected to fall by around 5-8C compared with Wednesday's peak.
Humidity will also ease, making it more comfortable for sleeping.
Even so, it will remain warm with temperatures still well above average, sitting in the mid- to high 20s Celsius into the weekend.
Heat to exacerbate conditions in driest regions
Paired with the significant heat, the lack of rain means dry ground and low soil moisture levels will continue to be of concern.
Whilst rain and then showers are forecast across Northern Ireland, Scotland and perhaps the far north of England, barely a millimetre is likely to fall.
By Friday and into the weekend, pressure will build across the southern half of the UK prolonging the dry spell further, despite a few showers continuing in the north.
An ongoing lack of rain means hosepipe bans are in force for millions of households and dry vegetation has provided fuel for wildfires to burn in a number of areas.
According to the Met Office, rainfall in England this month is at 4.4mm, one of the lowest levels on record - tied with June 1925 and behind only February 1891 when 3.3mm were recorded.
Wisley in Surrey has been one of the driest locations in south-east England, clocking up 42 days of no rain as of 29 July.
Rainfall levels in Wales, where drought was triggered in parts last week, are so low that July 2026 is currently the fourth driest of any month since records began.

Dairy farmers are installing "cow showers" and giant cooling fans as hotter, drier summers become more common.
Extreme heat has cut milk production by up to 20% and farmers are spending thousands of pounds to keep their cattle cool and protect milk yields.
Sarah Godwin's family have invested £15,000 in a ventilation and sprinkler system at their farm near Chippenham, Wiltshire, to help their animals cope with the "nearly continuous heatwave we are living through".
Professor Nicola Cannon from the Royal Agricultural University (RAU) in Cirencester says drought-hit grassland is also forcing many farmers to use winter feed earlier than planned.
More from Wiltshire
On a dairy farm near Swindon, Sam Woolford presses a switch on the wall of the milking parlour and 10 industrial-scale fans whirr into life.
"It's like a wind tunnel in here," he says.
It blows my hair back, like I'm riding a motorbike at speed.
The cows like it too, it seems, and crucially, they linger in the milking parlour, clearly cool and relaxed.
The system helps keep cattle comfortable during hot weather, but farmers say it cannot eliminate all of the effects of prolonged heat.
"Milk production is down by 20%," Prof Cannon says.
She explains that "cows feel stressed just as humans feel stressed when it's really hot and, as a response to that, their milk productivity goes down.
"So farmers are trying to help their cows, by putting in big fans, or sprinkler systems, to just try and cool animals down."
No grass in the pasture
Experts say prolonged dry weather is now becoming a regular challenge for dairy farms, leaving grass scorched, cattle heat-stressed and farmers relying on winter feed months earlier than planned.
"What we used to think of as extreme weather, we increasingly consider as normal." says Mike Kendon, a climate scientist at the Met Office., external
In Somerset, farmers have described this as the worst drought in 50 years, leaving crops struggling.
"Look at this stemmy nonsense," says Woolford, holding a bunch of thin grass towards me.
"There's no leaf to it, they don't get any nutritional quality from this rubbish."
His family have farmed dairy cows just outside Swindon for five generations.
They have seen hot summers and wet ones, but now Woolford, aged 20, and his dad and grandad have noticed a permanent change in the weather.
"We're praying it's not going to become the new norm," he says.
"But it looks like it will recur.
"It's really tough. The cows don't enjoy it, we're down on milk production by 20%, we just need some rain for the grass."
"Basically, soils are parched," explains Prof Cannon.
"There's people quoting 38, 39 days without rainfall now.
"We call that 'permanent wilting point'. Grass can't rebound after grazing, or after cutting for hay or silage."
Woolford's cows still come out into the fields in the morning, but by midday they are back in the barns, sheltering from the sun and eating feedstocks that should have been saved for the winter.
Last year this was news; this year, it is standard practice across west country dairy farming.
Down the road near Chippenham, Godwin's family have gone a step further, installing a network of what they call 'cow showers'- sprinklers that douse the cattle with cool water.
"Farming has got very hard recently," Godwin says.
"It seems like one long heatwave this summer."
The whole system cost £15,000 and "a lot of elbow grease and hard work" to install but it is not unique.
Why go farming?
Even ice cream producers are having a tough time.
Just north of Bath, Marshfield Farm churns out some of the West Country's best-known ice creams using milk from its own herd.
Rory Hawkins helps manage the herd that produces all the milk.
"The summers are getting hotter, which is great for the ice cream sales," he explains.
"But it affects the cows with heat stress, and we lose a lot of milk through the hotter summers now."
Hawkins, 27, is one of three children working in the family business.
Speaking to him and Woolford, aged just 20, I wonder why they would commit to a life in dairy farming.
All the Met Office experts agree that these hot summers will be more common, grass will be harder to grow, cows will need cooling down.
"I love working outside, helping look after the animals," Hawkins says.
"Weather is changing, but we just have to crack on with it."
Woolford agrees it is the "variety" of farm work that keeps him interested.
On his farm, I also meet Lara Browne, whose family run a farm near Trowbridge.
"You just have to make the best of the situation, and make your farm as resilient as you can," she says.
While many in their 20s often worry about the changing climate, these young farmers seem determined just to change the way they farm, and get on with it.
"I've not got any kids," Browne says, "but I feel like I'm already farming for the next generation."

Bakersfield officials warn residents to plan now as extreme heat rises
BAKERSFIELD, Calif.(KBAK/KBFX) — As temperatures climb, local health and safety officials are urging residents to plan ahead for extreme heat, especially for children and older adults who face higher risks.
“You definitely want to have a plan ahead of the heat,” said Dr. Kenyatta Evans with Bakersfield Memorial Hospital.
Evans said extreme heat can create extra risks for vulnerable groups, including children and older adults. “It’s because they heat up a lot more quickly than the rest of us do, and they don’t necessarily recognize the fact that they’re heating up so quickly,” she said.
Evans said signs of heat-related illness can include dry lips, slowing down, fatigue and needing more breaks. More serious symptoms include confusion, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and changes in behaviors. “Those are reasons to get to your emergency department right away,” Evans said.
Evans also recommends keeping water nearby during extreme heat. Officials said it can also help to keep other essentials ready in an emergency go-bag.
“Are you someone that needs to have eye glasses, making sure you have a spare pair there? Are there medications that you take? You would also want to keep some of that — a reserve of that in your go bag as well in addition to maybe a small amount of cash and copies of important documents,” said Andrew Freeborn with the Kern County Fire Department.
Freeborn also encouraged homeowners to take steps to protect their property during hot temperatures and dry conditions. “By creating defensible space, it minimizes the chances of a fire actually occurring on the property,” he said.
Creating defensible space includes removing vegetation and other materials that could start a fire or help it spread to a home.
Preparing a home for heat can also make a difference. PG&E said one way to keep a home cooler is to use the cooler parts of the day to your advantage.
“Open your windows in the early morning when it’s cooler, then close your windows, blinds and drapes as temperatures rise to keep that cool air inside for as long as possible before having to run your AC,” said Jeff Smith with PG&E.
When using air conditioning, Smith recommends setting the thermostat to 78 degrees when home and 85 degrees when away for two or more hours.

Wednesday will be downright sunny and warm from early on. “Holidaymakers would therefore do well to find a spot by the water early, as a tropically hot day is on the agenda,” Weeronline meteorologist Berend van Straaten said. Thermometers could hit 30 degrees before noon.
The RIVM’s National Heat Plan is in effect for the provinces of Limburg, North Brabant, Gelderland, and Overijssel. It is the third time this summer that the heat plan has been activated.
The weather service expects today to break the record for the hottest July 29 ever recorded. Temperatures will eventually rise to 30 degrees along the beaches, 33 degrees in the center of the country, and up to 35 degrees along the eastern border. Only the Wadden Islands won’t get tropical weather today, but they will get close, with maximums around 28 degrees.
This evening will be warm and clear, and overnight temperatures will not drop below 18 degrees in most places. “Right by the coast and in urban areas, it will be a sticky night, with minimum temperatures around or even well above 20 degrees.”
Thursday will be sunny and warm up rapidly after a warm night. “Tomorrow afternoon will be fully summery again, although there will be large temperature differences,” Van Straaten said. A westerly wind will bring less warm air into the country, and the western coast will see afternoon temperatures of around 22 degrees. It will be about 26 degrees in Amsterdam, and 28 degrees in Utrecht. The eastern half will get another tropical day, with maximums between 30 and 33 degrees.
“In the vast majority of places, the afternoon will be dry with a mix of sun and clouds, but later in the afternoon, a single shower (or thunderstorm) cannot be ruled out in the east and southeast.”
Friday will be considerably cooler, with temperatures of around 20 degrees right by the sea, 25 degrees in the center, and 30 degrees in some places in Limburg. “Cloud fields and sunny periods will alternate, and scattered rain or thunderstorms may develop across the country,” Van Straaten said. “However, these are local showers, meaning most places in the country will hardly notice them, or even not at all.”

Four weather systems are becoming active simultaneously over Gujarat, with rainy conditions expected to intensify again from 30 July.
The Meteorological Department has forecast heavy to very heavy rainfall across the state for the next six days, with North Gujarat, Central Gujarat and South Gujarat likely to witness intense showers.
Rainfall recorded in 25 talukas during morning hours
Between 6 am and 10 am today (29 July), rainfall was recorded in 25 talukas, with Sanjeli in Dahod receiving the highest rainfall of 1.38 inches. Lunawada in Mahisagar recorded around one inch of rainfall during the period.
In the 24-hour period from 6 am on July 28 to 6 am today, rainfall was reported in 27 talukas. Dahod received the highest rainfall of 18 mm (0.70 inches), while showers were also recorded in Dholka, Kaprada, Nanapondha and Subir talukas.
Dholera region submerged after heavy upstream rainfall
Heavy rainfall in the upstream areas of the Dholera region has led to water accumulation across several areas. Drone visuals showing widespread waterlogging have also surfaced, highlighting the impact of the ongoing monsoon spell.
Four rain systems active simultaneously
Four systems have become active in the state including Deep Depression, Monsoon Trough, Upper Air Cyclonic Circulation, and Western Disturbance.
Due to this, the intensity of rain will increase in the state. The rain system in Gujarat has also strengthened due to the effect of Deep Depression.
Rain intensity will increase from tomorrow
According to Weather Department Director Dr. A.K. Das, “The intensity of rain will increase from July 30, and heavy to very heavy rainfall has been forecast in South Gujarat.”
He added, “On July 31, extremely heavy to very heavy rainfall has been forecast in South Gujarat. Heavy rainfall has been forecast in Saurashtra and Central Gujarat. Heavy to very heavy rainfall has been forecast on August 1.”

Today, light to moderate rainfall with thunderstorms has been forecast across the state. However, tomorrow (30 July), an orange alert has been issued by the Meteorological Department for three districts in South Gujarat.
That means very heavy rainfall is likely in Narmada, Dang and Tapi. While heavy rainfall has been forecast in six districts including Vadodara, Surat, and Navsari.

The Assam government has announced a comprehensive relief package for people affected by the ongoing floods, introducing enhanced financial assistance, educational support and compensation measures aimed at assisting affected families across the state.
The Assam government has announced a comprehensive relief package for people affected by the ongoing floods, introducing enhanced financial assistance, educational support and compensation measures aimed at assisting affected families across the state.
Among the key measures, the government has waived the requirement of a post-mortem examination for disbursing ex-gratia assistance in flood-related deaths. The next of kin of deceased persons will be eligible to receive an ex-gratia of ₹4 lakh without the need for a post-mortem report.
Families of persons who have remained missing for more than 30 days due to the floods will also be eligible for an ex-gratia of ₹4 lakh, in accordance with the prescribed legal process.
In addition, the state government has announced ₹5 lakh in financial assistance from the Chief Minister's Relief Fund for the families of deceased persons. This amount will be provided over and above the ₹4 lakh ex-gratia assistance.
To provide immediate relief, more than 1 lakh severely flood-affected families will receive ₹15,000 each to meet essential household needs.
The government also announced that the Orunodoi scheme will resume from August 1, with beneficiaries in Charaideo, Jorhat, Golaghat and Sivasagar receiving ₹2,500 for the month of August.
Students in severely flood-affected districts will receive educational assistance beginning in August. The package includes book grants of ₹1,000 for higher secondary students, ₹3,000 for undergraduate students and ₹5,000 for postgraduate students. Free textbooks will also be provided to all school students, along with financial assistance for the purchase of school uniforms.
To ease the burden on students who lost academic documents in the floods, the government will reissue Class X and Class XII marksheets and certificates free of cost.
The state has further announced that assessment of damage to houses, livestock, fisheries and agricultural crops will commence from August 3, following which eligible families will receive compensation as per applicable norms.
The announcements form part of the state's ongoing flood relief and rehabilitation efforts as authorities continue to provide financial assistance and support for families affected by the monsoon disaster.

Monsoon returned vigorously on Tuesday to several parts of north India, including the national Capital, ending a spell of heat and energy-sapping humidity.

Seeking a first-hand view of the situation, Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta boarded a Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) bus on Tuesday and carried out an extensive on-ground inspection as heavy rain, thunderstorms and dark battered the Capital, prompting the India Meteorological Department (IMD) to upgrade its warning and issue a red alert.
The CM began the inspection from Jan Seva Sadan and travelled by bus via Outer Ring Road and Madhuban Chowk to the DDA Sports Complex in Sector 33, Rohini.
“The roads of the capital are not merely a means of transport but are also an integral part of Delhi’s identity, making their proper maintenance and safety essential. I also directed that road widening, repairs of damaged roads, and the filling of potholes be taken up on priority,” the CM said.
Accompanied by senior officials, she travelled along various routes to assess the city’s on-ground situation during the monsoon and review key works related to civic amenities. During the inspection, the CM reviewed waterlogging-prone areas, the cleanliness of major roads, and the condition of debris and garbage accumulated along roadsides.
Relentless rain through the morning inundated several parts of the city, with waterlogging reported from Connaught Place, Janpath, ITO, several roads in Lutyens’ Delhi, Bharat Mandapam Road, Barakhamba Road, Mathura Road near ITO, Kalindi Kunj and other low-lying areas.

Continuous downpour has led to airlines issuing travel advisories for passengers, warning of potential flight delays at the Indira Gandhi International (IGI) Airport.

The MCD said its central control room received 36 complaints between 2 pm and 6 pm, including reports of 20 waterlogging and 16 fallen tree complaints from several parts of the city.
